title: Campus Bikes
statement:
`workers[i] = [x, y]` is the grid position of worker `i` and `bikes[j] = [x, y]` is the position of bike `j`. There are at least as many bikes as workers, and no two of all these positions are the same.

Bikes are handed out greedily, one at a time. Consider every worker who has no bike yet together with every bike nobody has taken, and pick the pair with the smallest Manhattan distance `|x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|`. When several pairs share that distance, the pair with the lowest worker index wins, and if that still ties, the one with the lowest bike index. The chosen worker keeps the chosen bike; repeat until every worker has one.

Return an array `answer` of length `workers.length` where `answer[i]` is the 0-based index of the bike that worker `i` receives.
constraints: All worker and bike positions are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating the rule literally (scan every free worker–bike pair, take the closest, repeat) costs O(n²·m). Notice what the rule really does: it accepts pairs in increasing order of (distance, worker index, bike index), skipping any pair whose worker or bike is already used. A skipped pair can never become usable again, so a single pass over all pairs in that order reproduces the greedy exactly. Distances are whole numbers from 0 to 1998, so a bucket sort puts the pairs in order without comparisons.

## Approach

1. For every worker `w` (outer loop) and bike `b` (inner loop), compute the Manhattan `distance` and append `[w, b]` to `buckets[distance]`, growing `buckets` when needed. The loop order means each bucket is already ordered by worker, then by bike.
2. Fill `answer` with -1 (no bike yet), mark every bike as not `taken`, and set `assigned` to 0.
3. Visit the buckets from distance 0 upward, and the pairs inside each bucket in order.
4. Skip a pair when its worker already has a bike or its bike is taken.
5. Otherwise give bike `b` to worker `w`, mark it taken, and return as soon as `assigned` reaches the number of workers.

## Example 1, step by step

Worker 0 at `[0,0]` is 3 from bike 0 and 6 from bike 1; worker 1 at `[2,1]` is 2 from bike 0 and 3 from bike 1. So `buckets[2] = [[1,0]]`, `buckets[3] = [[0,0],[1,1]]` and `buckets[6] = [[0,1]]`. At distance 2, worker 1 takes bike 0. At distance 3, `[0,0]` is skipped (bike 0 is taken) and `[1,1]` is skipped (worker 1 is done). At distance 6, worker 0 takes bike 1, every worker is served, and the answer is `[1, 0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n·m + D), where D ≤ 1998 is the largest distance: each pair is bucketed once and looked at at most once. Sorting the pairs with a comparator instead gives O(n·m·log(n·m)).
- Space: O(n·m) for the bucketed pairs.

## Pitfalls

- Letting workers pick their nearest free bike in index order is wrong: a later worker who is closer to that bike must get it first (see worker 1 in Example 1).
- Ties go to the smaller worker index, then the smaller bike index. The worker-outer, bike-inner loop gives that order inside each bucket; a comparator sort must compare all three keys.
- Several pairs at the same distance can all be accepted, so keep scanning a bucket after an assignment.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `buckets` | `buckets[d]` lists the `[w, b]` pairs at distance `d`, in worker-then-bike order |
| `w`, `b` | a worker index and a bike index |
| `distance` | Manhattan distance between worker `w` and bike `b` |
| `answer` | `answer[w]` is worker `w`'s bike, or -1 while unassigned |
| `taken` | `taken[b]` is true once bike `b` is handed out |
| `assigned` | how many workers have a bike so far |

narration.5: ...and bikes in index order inside, so every bucket comes out ordered by worker, then by bike.

narration.7: Grow the bucket list until it has a slot for this distance.
narration.10: File the pair under its distance; this is the bucket sort.
narration.14: -1 marks a worker who has no bike yet.
narration.15: At the start no bike is taken.
narration.18: Go through the distances from the smallest upward.
narration.19: Within one distance, pairs arrive in worker-then-bike order, which is exactly the tie-break rule.
narration.20: If the worker already has a bike or the bike is gone, this pair can no longer be chosen...
narration.23: Otherwise this is the closest free pair: give bike b to worker w.
narration.26: Once every worker has a bike, the remaining pairs cannot change anything.
narration.27: Return the finished assignment straight away.
